_about: Each entry puts one known bug back into internal/lockop and the suite must fail. The package has one job -- keeping the three ways a lock can end apart (proved, asked-and-unprovable, nothing reached the desktop) -- so every mutant here collapses two of them into one, which is the failure the package was extracted to prevent: the terminal and the web page agreeing on a sentence the machine never produced. Run: python3 scripts/mutate.py scripts/mutations/lockop.json

mutants.note: an unconfirmed ask falls through to the hard-error branch, so the operator is told to fix a backend that did its job. The #965 three-way verdict collapses into two, and which way it collapses depends on the caller. TestAnUnconfirmedAskIsNeitherLockedNorFailed and its wrapped-error control.
the count says a session was locked while the outcome for that session says it was not, so the summary and the list disagree on one page. TestAConfirmedLockIsTheOnlyOutcomeThatSaysLocked.

the never-lock-the-wrong-thing rule is skipped and a greeter or a remote admin session is handed to the backend -- locking the greeter leaves an uninputtable wall, locking the remote one shuts the admin out of the machine. TestASessionThatCannotBeLockedIsCountedAndNeverTouched.
a refusal is itemised but not counted, so the summary reads "locked 0 of 0" while the list below it names a session. TestASessionThatCannotBeLockedIsCountedAndNeverTouched.

the refusal is recorded and then the session is locked anyway, so a manager session is both refused and asked, and the page shows it twice with opposite things said about it. TestASessionThatCannotBeLockedIsCountedAndNeverTouched.

the ownership filter inverted: locking one account asks the backend to lock every other account's sessions. The exact-match rule is also what keeps two accounts differing only by case apart. TestOwnedByTakesEverySessionOfThatAccountExactly.

the shortfall is silently subtracted instead of reported. The rows still reach the caller, so the page locks the sessions it happened to read and says nothing about the one it did not -- 'locked 1' about a census that lost a row, which is the reassurance a partial read has not earned. Re-pointed from `if err != nil { return nil, err }`, which #168 replaced: that pattern matching nothing is how a retired mutant looks green. TestAFailedSessionListingIsNotReportedAsNoSession, TestASessionListingThatReadNothingSaysItCouldNotLook

mutants.old: func (r Result) Asked() bool { return len(r.Outcomes) > 0 }
mutants.new: func (r Result) Asked() bool { return r.Locked > 0 }
mutants.note: "was anything touched" becomes "did anything lock", so a run where every session was refused or failed reports that nothing was asked -- and the caller that answers with an exit code reports success. TestAHardErrorIsNeitherLockedNorUnconfirmed.

mutants.old:
if err != nil && len(sessions) == 0 {
		return nil, err
mutants.new:
if err != nil {
		return nil, err
mutants.note: the rows are discarded before the handler ever sees them, which is where the lock page's 503 actually came from: one unreadable session costs every session the read did name. TestAFailedSessionListingIsNotReportedAsNoSession
